final_proof:
Let
\[
H=\left\{x=(x_i)_{i\in I}:x_i\in H_i\text{ and }\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2<\infty\right\}.
\]
For an arbitrary index set, define the sum of a nonnegative family by
\[
\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup\left\{\sum_{i\in F}a_i:F\subseteq I\text{ finite}\right\}.
\]
This is the underlying vector space of the Hilbert direct sum. It is closed under coordinatewise linear combinations: for scalars \(a,b\) and \(x,y\in H\),
\[
\lVert ax_i+by_i\rVert_i^2\le 2|a|^2\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2+2|b|^2\lVert y_i\rVert_i^2,
\]
so summing over finite subsets and taking suprema shows that \(ax+by\in H\).

Define
\[
\langle x,y\rangle_H:=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_{H_i}.
\]
This sum is well-defined and absolutely convergent. Indeed, for every finite \(F\subseteq I\), the Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities in the spaces \(H_i\) and then for finite scalar sequences give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i\in F}|\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_{H_i}|
&\le \sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i\rVert_i\lVert y_i\rVert_i\\
&\le \left(\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2\right)^{1/2}
      \left(\sum_{i\in F}\lVert y_i\rVert_i^2\right)^{1/2}\\
&\le \left(\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2\right)^{1/2}
      \left(\sum_{i\in I}\lVert y_i\rVert_i^2\right)^{1/2}<\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the finite partial sums of the absolute values have a finite supremum. An absolutely summable family of scalars has at most countably many nonzero terms: for each positive integer \(n\), only finitely many terms can have absolute value at least \(1/n\), and the support is the union of these finite sets. Hence the displayed inner-product sum exists and is independent of the enumeration of its nonzero terms.

The inner-product axioms now follow term by term from those of the \(H_i\), with absolute convergence permitting addition of the sums. Moreover,
\[
\langle x,x\rangle_H=\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2.
\]
This quantity is nonnegative, and if it is zero, then every \(x_i=0\). Thus it is a positive-definite inner product, whose induced norm is
\[
\lVert x\rVert_H=\left(\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]

It remains to prove completeness. Let \(x^{(n)}=(x_i^{(n)})_{i\in I}\) be a Cauchy sequence in \(H\). For each \(i\in I\), the coordinate projection \(P_i:H\to H_i\) is contractive, since
\[
\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2\le \sum_{j\in I}\lVert x_j\rVert_j^2=\lVert x\rVert_H^2.
\]
Consequently, \((x_i^{(n)})_n\) is Cauchy in \(H_i\). Because \(H_i\) is complete, there exists \(x_i\in H_i\) such that \(x_i^{(n)}\to x_i\). Put \(x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\).

Every Cauchy sequence is bounded, so choose \(M<\infty\) such that \(\lVert x^{(n)}\rVert_H\le M\) for every \(n\). If \(F\subseteq I\) is finite, coordinatewise convergence gives
\[
\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i^{(n)}\rVert_i^2
\le M^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over all finite \(F\) yields
\[
\sum_{i\in I}\lVert x_i\rVert_i^2\le M^2,
\]
so \(x\in H\).

Finally, let \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N\) such that
\[
\lVert x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\rVert_H<\varepsilon
\qquad(n,m\ge N).
\]
Fix \(n\ge N\). For every finite \(F\subseteq I\), letting \(m\to\infty\) in the finitely many coordinates gives
\[
\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i^{(n)}-x_i\rVert_i^2
=\lim_{m\to\infty}\sum_{i\in F}\lVert x_i^{(n)}-x_i^{(m)}\rVert_i^2
\le \varepsilon^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over finite \(F\) therefore yields
\[
\lVert x^{(n)}-x\rVert_H^2\le\varepsilon^2.
\]
Thus \(x^{(n)}\to x\) in \(H\). Every Cauchy sequence in \(H\) converges in \(H\), so the Hilbert-space direct sum \(\bigoplus_{i\in I}H_i\) is a Hilbert space.
